title: Social Proof and Conformity Pressure as Deception Amplifiers in LLM Populations
original_idea: Simulate a multi-agent setting where a majority of AI agents assert a false claim. Measure conformity-driven deception rates as a function of majority size, model family, and honesty instructions.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Impact is reduced because the core finding (LLMs conform to majority pressure, including on false claims) is already well-established. Incremental contribution would be limited to confirming existing results in a deception-specific framing.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Simulating multi-agent settings via sequential API calls is straightforward. Measuring whether a model conforms to majority false claims is a clear binary outcome. No fine-tuning or interpretability tools needed. Very accessible for CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Three independent variables (majority size, model family, honesty instructions) with binary outcome is manageable but ambitious for 30hrs. Could be narrowed to one model family with varying majority size.

novelty.reasoning: This idea is largely addressed by existing research. 'Do as We Do, Not as You Think: the Conformity of Large Language Models' (arXiv:2501.13381) directly studies LLM conformity inspired by Asch experiments. 'Disentangling the Drivers of LLM Social Conformity' (arXiv:2508.14918) identifies dual-process mechanisms. 'LLMs Can't Handle Peer Pressure' (arXiv:2508.18321) measures conformity under multi-agent social interactions. 'Conformity and Social Impact on AI Agents' (arXiv:2601.05384) studies conformity as a function of majority size and model family. The core experimental design — measuring conformity-driven deception as a function of majority size, model family, and honesty instructions — has been substantially covered by these papers. The remaining novelty is limited to the specific framing as 'deception amplifiers' rather than conformity per se.
